Here is a polished version of the text:

---

They believed the field was going to waste, and so they gathered the marker rocks and stones and piled them into a barn. They say the rocks were shaped—some of them scratched with triangles and other forms—as though someone had been trying to invent a new language. They say the rocks went to build that wall over there, guarding the manor, and that a few were used for the state house. The crops refused to grow.

I say the stones marked an old tongue, and it was called *eternity*, and it pointed toward the river. I say that after that collection, no pillow in the big house ever dreamed again. I say that somewhere beneath this ground moulders one called Alice, whose great-grandson is old now too, and who refuses to speak of slavery. I say that at the master's table, only one plate is set for supper. I say no seed can flourish on this ground, once planted and then forsaken. Wild berries warm a field of bones. Bloom how you must, I say.

---

# The Field of Stones

Workers moved across the field gathering marker rocks and stones from land they believed was wasting away, useless and barren. One by one, they piled the stones into a barn, clearing the ground of what they took to be nothing more than scattered debris.

Yet the rocks were not ordinary. Each bore careful carvings—triangles and other deliberate forms etched into their surfaces. These markings suggested something greater than random weathering: they hinted at an intention, an attempt to create or preserve a language, a message left behind by hands long gone.

The collected stones did not remain in the barn. They were repurposed, put to practical use by those who saw only building material where meaning had once been inscribed. Some were laid into a wall to guard the manor; others were carried away to construct the state house, their ancient markings sealed into the foundations of power and property.

But the narrator insists otherwise. These stones, he maintains, were never meaningless. They marked an ancient language—one called *eternity*—and their carvings pointed always toward the river, as if guiding the living toward something enduring and sacred.

For the ground itself is no ordinary field. It is a burial place, holding the dead beneath its soil—including one named Alice. Here, no planted seed can flourish; the earth refuses cultivation. Only wild berries bloom across the surface, dark fruit rising over a field of bones, a quiet testament to the forgotten lives resting beneath.
outputs.L4:
# The Language of Stones

They called them field stones—nothing more. The rough, marked rocks that dotted the earth were, in their eyes, mere obstacles to progress, debris to be cleared away and repurposed. But I say they were wrong. I say those stones held meaning that ran deeper than any plow could reach.

I say these were not simple rocks scattered by chance across the landscape. Each one bore the careful markings of hands long silenced, hands that had inscribed upon their surfaces an ancient language—a testament to lives lived, loves lost, and souls that yearned for something beyond their bondage. In the weathered grooves and deliberate scratches, I read the word *eternity*, carved by those who possessed nothing else to leave behind but their insistence on being remembered.

To those who dismissed them, these were worthless things—inconvenient stones cluttering fertile ground. So they gathered them up. They broke apart what had been so carefully placed. They used these sacred markers—these headstones of the enslaved—to build their walls and raise their buildings, mortaring memory into the foundations of their prosperity, never pausing to consider what they were desecrating.

But the land remembers, even when people choose to forget.

I say a curse settled upon that ground the moment those stones were torn away. The fields turned barren, refusing to yield their bounty to those who had stolen from the dead. The walls they built seemed to whisper in the night; the buildings held a chill no fire could warm. For you cannot construct a home upon the bones of the forgotten and expect to sleep in peace. You cannot erase a people's final resting place and escape the weight of what you have done.

This violence—this theft not only of life but of the right to be mourned, to be remembered—cannot be forgotten. I say it cannot be forgiven. The desecration of the dead is a wound that does not close, a debt that cannot be paid, a silence that screams across generations demanding to be heard.

And yet—

Even from this field of bones, life stubbornly returns. Green shoots push through the disturbed and cursed soil, wildflowers bloom where markers once stood, and something persists that refuses to be entirely buried. It is not forgiveness that blooms there, but memory itself, insistent and alive, reclaiming what others tried to erase.

I say these stones spoke a language. I say they still do.

# They Thought They Knew

They thought the old house at the end of the lane was empty. For years, the children of the neighborhood had passed by its crooked gate, whispering stories about broken windows and creaking floors. They thought the shadows in the upstairs rooms were nothing more than the wind playing tricks with the tattered curtains.

But they were wrong.

They thought the caretaker had left decades ago, taking with him every trace of life that once filled those halls. They thought the garden, overgrown and wild, had been surrendered entirely to the weeds and the crows. Yet if any of them had paused long enough to truly look, they might have noticed the single window on the second floor that was always spotlessly clean.

They thought the truth was simple, because simple answers are comfortable. It is easier to believe a house is abandoned than to imagine someone choosing to remain hidden inside it. It is easier to invent ghosts than to confront the loneliness of a person the world has forgotten.

One autumn evening, a curious girl named Elena decided to test what everyone else merely assumed. She climbed the sagging porch steps, her heart pounding, and knocked on the weathered door. For a long moment, nothing happened. They thought the house would answer with silence, as it always had.

Then the door opened.

An elderly woman stood in the doorway, her eyes bright with surprise and something like hope. "I've been waiting a very long time," she said softly, "for someone to stop believing the stories and simply ask."

And in that instant, Elena understood something the others never had: sometimes the things we are most certain about are exactly the things we never bothered to question.

They thought they knew the whole story.

They had only ever known the beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about an unmarked slave burial ground discovered when landowners cleared what they thought was an empty field, using the repeated phrase "i say" as a counter-voice to "they say."
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Field Held

They say the field was empty. I say the field was full—full of the ones who tilled it, full of the ones who fell into it, full of the ones who became it.

They say they found nothing but stones. I say those stones were placed by hands that trembled in the dark, hands that could not carve a name but knew a name, hands that pressed one flat rock upon the earth so that a mother's boy would not be lost to the leveling grass.

They say the ground was unmarked. I say the ground remembered. I say the ground kept every count the ledgers never kept, kept the weight of every body pressed into its keeping, kept the shape of every mouth that opened and closed and opened and was silenced.

They say: clear it. I say: what you call clearing, I call unearthing. What you call empty, I call waiting. What you call progress, I call the long patience of the buried, who did not consent to be forgotten and did not consent to be found, but who are here, still here, always were here, under the boot and under the blade and under the bright indifferent afternoon.

They say the deed shows only their name. I say the soil shows other names, older names, the names that were traded and the names that were beaten out and the names that survived only as the ache in a great-granddaughter's hip, the names that come back now like water finding its old riverbed.

They say: it was so long ago. I say: touch the ground and tell me when. I say: time is a story the comfortable tell. I say: the dead do not keep our calendars. They keep their own hours, and the hour is now, and the field is speaking, and I have stopped, at last, to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a haunting stream-of-consciousness poem contrasting what colonizers "say" versus what the buried "say" about a desecrated African American graveyard where crops now refuse to grow.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Ground Remembers

They say

*progress,* they say
*development,* they say
the land was empty, was fallow, was
*nobody's*—

but the buried say
*we were somebody's,*
say *mother,* say *son sold south,*
say *my name was,* say *my name was,*
say the ledger never learned to spell us right—

they say
turn the soil, break the clay, plant the season's promise
in neat commercial rows,
say *this dirt is only dirt,*
say the deed is clean, the title
clear—

but the buried say
*we are the clearing you keep clearing,*
say *dig and you will meet us,*
say *root and you will feel us,*
holding, holding
what you tried to plow under—

they say
*why won't it grow,*
say *bad seed,* say *drought,* say *God's own
mystery,*
scratch their heads above the barren furrows—

but the buried say
*we will not feed
what refused to feed us,*
say *we are done being
harvest,*
say *let the corn refuse,
let the cotton close its fist,
let the fields lie down
and testify—*

they say
*forget,*
say *that was long ago,*
say *let bygones,* say *move on,*
pave a parking lot, pour the smooth
forgetting—

but the buried say
*we are the crack that comes
in every concrete season,*
say *we are the weed
of remembering,*
say *speak our names
and something might grow again,*
say *say them,*
say

*say them.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical passage where marked stones represent a lost language of the enslaved, weaving in imagery of a woman named Alice, a master's table, and wild berries blooming over bones.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Marking Stones

They found her language in the yard,
where Alice pressed her secrets hard
into the river stones—each mark
a syllable of holy dark,
a grammar no white hand could read,
a scripture sown from stolen seed.

By day she served the master's table,
poured his wine, kept smooth the sable
silence of her downcast eyes,
while underneath her apron lies
a pocket full of speaking stones—
her mother tongue, her mothers' bones.

*Nyame,* whispered into flint.
*Freedom,* in a rust-red tint.
She etched the names they tried to drown,
passed them hand to trembling hand,
buried grammar in the ground
where no ledger, no command,
could reach the roots of what they'd sown—
a nation carved in whispered stone.

And where they laid the nameless down,
where earth accepts what earth has grown,
the wild blackberries climb and bloom,
their dark fruit swelling from the loom
of ribs and clavicles and skulls—
each berry sweet where mourning dulls,

as if the dead themselves had learned
to speak in sugar, having earned
a tongue no whip could cut away.
And Alice, on her final day,
lay down among the stones she'd made
and let the berry-shadows braid

her story into vine and root—
*Read me,* said the ripening fruit.
*Read me,* said the marking stone.
*You are not, and were not, alone.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about historical erasure and slavery, told through fragmented testimony, ending with an image of berries growing in a field of bones and a command to "bloom how you must."
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Ledger Kept**

They wrote us down in columns—
*one man, prime*, *one woman, breeding*,
a price where a name should be.
The rest is water damage,
is the page they did not turn to,
is the mouth the record closed.

—my mother was called—
                        (here the paper tears)
—and she braided into my scalp a map
of somewhere we had not seen but knew
the way you know a song
                        before the words.

*Item.* *Item.* *Item.*
The auctioneer counted us like coins
and history agreed to the accounting,
stamped it, filed it, called it *fact*—

but I remember the field.
I remember the sound the whole crew made
low, under breath, a hum
they could not tax or measure,
                        the one thing
                        never entered in a book.

They buried us at the tree line
so the crop would not be interrupted.
No stones. The overseer said
stones cost money and we did not.

                        (here the archive ends)
                        (here the historians shrug)
                        (here the silence does its work)

But listen—

Come spring, at the edge of that old field,
the bramble found the marrow
and made something red of it.
Berries thick as testimony,
sweet on the tongue that stole us,
rooted in the ones
they thought they had unwritten.

So to every seed that fell
through the cracks of what they saved,
to every name the ledger swallowed—

you who were counted and not kept,
kept and not counted:

                        bloom how you must.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
